title: Polygon Partitioning
notes: Open by framing partitioning as a preprocessing chapter. The point is not to admire cuts for their own sake; it is to trade one arbitrary polygon for pieces with simpler geometry, so triangulation, visibility, and convex processing become easier to reason about and implement.

title: From Arbitrary Polygon To Algorithm-Friendly Pieces
notes: Use this slide as the contract for the lecture. Each named structure removes a kind of ambiguity: monotone pieces remove disconnected sweep slices, trapezoids expose supports, mountains make ears obvious, and convex pieces are the shape many downstream algorithms really want.

title: Whole-Polygon Triangulation Versus Cut-First Strategy
notes: Make the comparison concrete: partitioning is not competing with triangulation so much as preparing for it. A cut-first strategy isolates the difficult sweep events, then asks each resulting piece to satisfy a stronger geometric promise before triangulation or convex processing begins.

title: Y-Monotone Polygons: Horizontal Lines See One Interval
notes: Spend time on the horizontal-line test because it is the chapter's most useful mental model. A monotone polygon can still be nonconvex, but the sweep never has to maintain two disconnected interior intervals for the same piece.

title: Interior Cusps Split A Sweep Interval
notes: Point to the two highlighted notches and ask what a horizontal sweep remembers just before and just after those levels. The important observation is local: a cusp is where the connected slice bookkeeping changes, so it is a natural place to insert a diagonal.

title: Reflex Vertices Whose Neighbors Lie On One Side
notes: Separate two ideas that students often merge. Reflex means the internal angle bends inward; cusp means that inward bend matters to the chosen sweep direction. The same vertex can be harmless for one direction and troublesome for another.

title: Monotone Triangulation: Sorted Vertices And A Stack
notes: Do not turn this into a full code lecture; keep it as algorithmic intuition. Once vertices are sorted by height, the stack represents the unresolved visible frontier. Monotonicity is exactly what prevents the frontier from branching into several independent intervals.

title: Trapezoidalization: Supports And Active Edge Order
notes: Explain the data-structure role of trapezoidalization. Sorting supplies the event order, while the active edge structure answers the geometric question: if a cusp shoots a support ray horizontally, which boundary edge does it encounter first?

title: From Supports To Monotone Pieces
notes: Connect this slide directly to the previous one. A support line is not the final goal; it is evidence for where a diagonal can remove the cusp event. Once the pieces all pass the monotone test, the triangulation problem has changed character.

title: Sort, Sweep, Connect Cusps, Triangulate Pieces
notes: This is the operational slide. The chapter is not asking students to memorize every low-level case; it asks them to see why sorting and active-edge order locate the supports, and why the resulting monotone pieces make the remaining triangulation routine simple.

title: Monotone Mountains: A Base Plus One Convex Chain
notes: Describe mountains as a useful extreme of monotonicity. The base anchors the polygon, and the upper chain is convex enough that ear choices become visually forced. That makes mountains a clean bridge between monotone partitioning and linear triangulation.

title: Mountain Ear Lemma: Convex Chain Vertices Can Be Removed
notes: Use the colored triangles to make the lemma feel geometric rather than magical. The convex chain bends the right way, so an ear triangle does not poke outside the polygon. After clipping it, the remaining polygon is again a smaller mountain.

title: Linear Mountain Triangulation
notes: The purpose of the fan diagram is not to claim every mountain is triangulated by the same fan. It is to show the count and the local nature of the operation: each accepted ear produces one triangle, and no vertex needs repeated global reconsideration.

title: Linear-Time Triangulation: Chazelle And Seidel
notes: Keep the history balanced. Chazelle proves that linear triangulation is possible, while Seidel gives a randomized path that is important in computational geometry practice. For this lecture, their role is to show that partitioning is part of a larger search for exploitable polygon structure.

title: Reflex Vertices Control Lower And Upper Bounds
notes: Use the ledger language deliberately. Reflex vertices are the debt that convex partitioning must pay down. The lower bound says one piece cannot hide too many reflex difficulties, while the upper bound says a simple constructive process can always stay within r plus one pieces.

title: Hertel-Mehlhorn: Triangulate, Then Remove Inessential Diagonals
notes: Close by tying the chapter together. Hertel-Mehlhorn is memorable because it begins with something easy to trust, a triangulation, and then deletes only diagonals whose removal has a local convexity certificate. That is the same chapter theme: add or remove structure when a geometric invariant says it is safe.
